rewritten_text:
We were united in our love for Adrian, though she, still scarcely beyond childhood, could neither comprehend his merits as fully as I did nor share my sympathy with his interests and beliefs. I was constantly beside him. Such tenderness and sensitivity belonged to his nature that our conversations acquired a gentle, almost otherworldly quality. At other times he was merry as a lark singing from its tower in the sky, eagle-like in the flight of his thoughts, and innocent as a dove with quiet eyes. He could banish Perdita's solemnity and soothe the painful restlessness of my own character. I remembered my turbulent wishes and bitter contests with other people as one remembers an uneasy dream. I seemed transformed, as though my soul had passed into another body, whose new senses and arrangement of nerves changed the image of the visible world reflected in the mind. Yet this was not so: my strength remained, along with my urgent longing for sympathy and my desire for vigorous action. My manly virtues had not abandoned me, for the enchantress Urania left Sampson's locks untouched as he rested at her feet; everything, however, had become gentler and more humane. Nor was Adrian's teaching confined to the impersonal truths of philosophy and history. While using these to help me master my rash and untutored spirit, he also unfolded before me the living book of his heart, allowing me to understand and feel its extraordinary nature.

England's former queen had tried, even from her son's infancy, to plant bold and ambitious purposes in his mind. Recognizing his genius and exceptional abilities, she nurtured them with the intention of later employing them to advance her own designs. She fostered his hunger for learning and his headlong courage. Even his ungovernable attachment to freedom she endured, hoping it would develop, as it too often does, into an appetite for power. She sought to rear him in resentment of those responsible for his father's abdication and in a determination to avenge himself upon them. Here she failed. However distorted the accounts he received, the story of a great and wise nation claiming its right to self-government awakened his admiration. He became a republican by conviction while still young. His mother nevertheless refused to despair. To her love of authority and proud consciousness of noble birth she joined resolute ambition, patience, and self-command. She applied herself to understanding her son's disposition. Through praise, rebuke, and persuasion she searched for the strings that would answer her touch. Though the music she produced sounded discordant to her ears, she rested her hopes upon his gifts and remained certain she would eventually win him over.

For that reason, I decided to get out as soon as we reached the town and move beyond his hearing. I managed this successfully. My small traveling case lay in the luggage compartment beneath my feet, and I only had to lift a hinged cover to reach it. I tossed it down ahead of me, climbed down after it, and found myself beside the town's first streetlamp, on its first stretch of pavement. The convicts continued in the coach. I knew where they would be hurried away to the river. In my imagination I saw the boat and its convict crew waiting at the slime-covered steps. Once again I heard the rough order, “Start rowing, you!” as though the men were dogs. Once again I saw that wicked Noah's Ark resting on the black water.

I could not have explained what frightened me. My fear had no clear object or shape, but it was powerful. Walking toward the hotel, I trembled with a dread far greater than the mere worry of an unpleasant or painful recognition. I am sure it never became anything definite. For a few minutes, the terror of my childhood had simply returned.

The coffee room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had ordered dinner and even sat down to eat before the waiter recognized me. After apologizing for his poor memory, he asked whether he should send the boot-cleaning servant to fetch Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said. “Certainly not.”

The waiter looked surprised. He was the same man who had delivered the commercial travelers' great complaint on the day I became an apprentice. At his first opportunity, he placed a dirty old local newspaper so directly before me that I picked it up and read this paragraph:

Our readers may be interested to hear more about the recent, romantic good fortune of a young local ironworker. What a subject, incidentally, for the magical pen of TOOBY, our newspaper's poet, whose greatness our town has yet to acknowledge fully! The young man's first supporter, companion, and friend was a highly respected gentleman with some connection to the grain and seed business. His exceptionally spacious and convenient business premises stand within a hundred miles of the High Street. We confess to a personal pleasure in identifying HIM as the Mentor to our young Telemachus, the guide behind his success. It is gratifying to know that our own town produced the man who laid the foundations of this young man's fortune.

And I call upon you, spirits of the dead, and you, wandering agents of revenge, to help and guide me in my task. Let that accursed, hellish monster suffer agony to its depths. Let him experience the despair that now consumes me.”

I had begun this invocation solemnly, filled with an awe that almost convinced me the spirits of my murdered friends could hear and approve my dedication. By the end, however, the furies had taken hold of me, and rage choked off my words.

A loud, demonic laugh answered me through the silence of the night. It rang heavily and lingeringly in my ears, echoing among the mountains, until I felt that all of hell surrounded me with ridicule and laughter. Surely I would have gone mad at that moment and ended my wretched life, had my vow not been heard and my life preserved for revenge. As the laughter faded, a familiar, detested voice seemed to whisper audibly right beside my ear: “I am satisfied, miserable creature! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.”

I sprang toward the place the sound had come from, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly the broad moon rose, casting its full light on his hideous, misshapen figure as he fled faster than any human could.

I chased him, and for many months the pursuit has been my only occupation. Following a faint clue, I traced the winding course of the Rhone, to no purpose. I reached the blue Mediterranean, where an extraordinary chance allowed me to see the fiend steal aboard a ship at night and conceal himself. The vessel was bound for the Black Sea. I booked passage on that same ship, but he escaped by means I still cannot explain.

Across the wilderness of Tartary and Russia I have kept following his trail, although he has continued to elude me. Sometimes peasants, terrified by his horrible appearance, told me which way he had gone. Sometimes he left signs himself to guide me, fearing that if I lost him altogether, I would give in to despair and die. Snow fell upon my head, and on the white plain I could see the marks of his enormous footsteps. You are only beginning your life; worry is new to you, and agony unknown. How can you understand what I have suffered and still suffer? Cold, deprivation, and exhaustion were the smallest torments I was destined to bear. Some devil had cursed me, and I carried my everlasting hell wherever I went. Yet a benevolent spirit still followed and guided my steps. At the moments when I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly rescue me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger left my body too exhausted to go on, a meal awaited me in the wilderness, restoring both my strength and my spirits.
